title: Is Silicon Valley becoming the new Hollywood?
text:
Is Silicon Valley becoming the new Hollywood?

# Is Silicon Valley becoming the new Hollywood? 

 Published 11 January 2019 6:00am GMT 

 Jeff Bezos files for divorce from wife MacKenzie Bezos after 25 years of marriage Credit: Jerod Harris/Getty Images North America 

 Published 11 January 2019 6:00am GMT 

In May 2017, a grainy photograph of a little boy with a blonde fringe, a toothy grin, slightly sticking out ears and braces on his trousers was posted on Twitter. The boy’s arm was slung lovingly around his mother. The picture, shared by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, was captioned simply: “I won the lottery with my mom. Thanks for literally everything.”

Today, that little boy is 54; he has lost the fringe (plus the rest of his hair), and has morphed into the richest man on Earth. 

This week, the end of his marriage to MacKenzie Bezos has put him in the headlines. But, in truth, this son of a teenage mother has rarely been out of them in recent years. 

Having started his world-dominating online retailer from his garage in Seattle in 1994, the boy - who loved not only his mother but also Star Trek and science - grew up to create an estimated $137 billion (£107 billion) fortune for himself. If split equally during his forthcoming divorce proceedings, the sum could make his soon-to-be ex-wife the world’s richest woman. 

Given that they married in 1993, a year before the birth of Amazon, you might argue that she has won the marriage lottery. Though it should be noted that novelist MacKenzie is award-winning in her own career,and worked with Bezos on his business, becomnig one of Amazon’s earliest employees. 

If the attention devoted to their split and the rumours surrounding it - Bezos had allegedly been conducting an affair with former television anchor Lauren Sanchez - is reminiscent of that given to such break-ups as Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie’s, or Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin’s, it is hardly surprising. As Silicon Valley royalty, Bezos is part of a new set of superstars. Where, in the last century, Hollywood dominated in the cultural stakes, the 21st century is all about a rather different elite: the Technorati. 

 Elon Musk (L) and his then-wife Talulah Riley Credit: David M. Benett/ Getty Images Europe 

As far as comparisons go, the two sets have far more in common than their California locale. In a relatively short time, the Technorati have become the demigods of modern life, rulers of a shiny new kingdom that spans the Santa Clara Valley, with the city of Palo Alto at its epicentre. 

Like Hollywood, it has taken on the status of a dream factory for those aspiring to make it big, and quick. Just as the advent of the moving picture brought a flood of hopeful would-be stars and starlets to Tinseltown, so the rapid transposition of the whole of human life to the web has brought an influx of ambitious tech-heads to the area that sits just 350 miles to the north of the Hollywood hills. 

And for many, the rewards have been great. The rise and rise of the tech billionaire has brought us, among others, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg (net worth £56 billion), Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates (net worth £71 billion), Snapchat co-founder Evan Spiegel (worth £3.2 billion) and Google co-founder Larry Page (net worth £39 billion). 

“We weren’t cool,” Snapchat co-founder Bobby Murphy once told Forbes, “so we tried to build things to be cool.” 

It’s like a high school movie plotline writ large: the geeks shall inherit the earth. And in doing so they shall become desirable and revered to a degree that no-one could foresee. Suddenly, they were marrying actual celebrities (see Spiegel’s nuptials to supermodel Miranda Kerr, or Tesla co-founder Elon Musk’s to actress Talulah Riley) and revelling in their newfound wealth. Bezos, who did not at first spend his profits lavishly, now owns a Gulfstream jet besides homes in Seattle, Washington, Beverly Hills and New York.

As Brad Stone writes in his 2013 book The Everything Store: Jeff Bezos and The Age of Amazon: “In the late 1990s, the Web evolved from the province of geeks to the stuff of front-page newspaper stories, day traders, and regular folks who were venturing for the first time into what was then popularly called cyberspace...In Silicon Valley, entrepreneurs and their backers got drunk on the overflowing optimism and abundant venture capital.”

For those who got it right, the money to be made was staggering; as life-changing as becoming a film star. Not for nothing has Silicon Valley been termed the “billionaire factory.”

 Miranda Kerr (left) and her Snapchat CEO husband Evan Spiegel Credit: OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP 

But whereas image is everything in movieland, the men (and they were largely men) behind the tech firms took longer to break out of the shadows and use their newfound wealth to transform themselves. Look at another photo of Bezos - a portrait taken in 1997, the year that Amazon went public - and you’ll see the kind of unassuming figure at whom no-one would look twice in the street. Dressed in blue shirt and brown trousers, he perches awkwardly between piles of books, smiling benignly.

Two decades later, his physical metamorphosis is stark. Appearing at a conference in 2017, he was pictured with bulging biceps straining out from beneath a black polo shirt, aviator-style sunglasses clamped to his face. That he looked more than a little like the film star Vin Diesel did not go unnoticed.

Perhaps it’s too much of a stretch to say that the geeks of Silicon Valley were becoming the new pin-ups, but when Spiegel graced the cover of the men’s edition of Italian Vogue two years earlier, the proposition suddenly didn’t seem so far-fetched.

And as the status of the Technorati evolved to match that of their Hollywood counterparts, so did their lifestyles. For some this meant joining private members’ clubs like The Modernist in downtown San Francisco, known as an exclusive hang-out for Silicon Valley’s tech elite. With fees reported to be as much as $3,000 (£2,350) a year, it’s hard to image who else could afford it. 

As in Hollywood, there is also a fixation on wellness (this is California, after all.) The late-night pizzas that sustained those behind the early start-ups have since given way to veganism and meditation pods, in what we might call the ‘Goopification’ of the Valley, to borrow from Paltrow’s lifestyle brand.

In December, for the second year running, Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey visited a retreat to practice Vipassana meditation - an ancient pre-Buddhist technique that involves 10 days of silence, almost every minute of it spent in quiet reflection. He also likes to meditate for half an hour at 5am each morning.

 Twitter's Jack Dorsey Credit: Phillip Faraone/ Getty Images North America 

Which is not to say there hasn’t also been a culture of excess, and in some cases even debauchery. In her 2018 book, which examined the so-called “boys’ club” of Silicon Valley, Emily Chang exposed the “drug-heavy, sex-heavy” parties that take place in some of the mansions of the Technorati. In describing the “freewheeling sex lives pursued by men in tech” and the consequences for the women involved, she recalled the spiritual link between the original hippies of the Bay Area, back in the sexually liberated (for some) 1960s. Both saw themselves as free-thinking disruptors who were forging a brave new world. 

And where those countercultural pioneers took LSD to expand their minds, some of the tech elite have also taken - albeit it in far smaller quantities, known as “microdosing”, to sharpen theirs. As Cambridge academics Barbara Sahakian, Camilla d’Angelo and George Savulich wrote last year, “growing number of young professionals in Silicon Valley insist that taking small doses of psychedelic drugs simply makes them perform better at work – becoming more creative and focused.”

But drug use is not confined to the pursuit of the next billion dollar idea. At the end of last year, Colin Kroll, 34 the co-founder of Vine and an app called HQ Trivia, was found dead in his New York apartment. Police were reported to have found drugs paraphernalia near his body. 

While the tech revolution has changed our lives more profoundly than anything in recent history, the dizzying success of those behind it has played out, in many ways, like that of Hollywood’s biggest names. 

Unlike the stars of the big screen, the Technorati are not there to make us love them; they are there to make us love their products. But their influence is no less great. And, as Oscar Wilde once said, “It is better to have a permanent income than to be fascinating.” The hard-nosed, moneymaking “lottery winners” of Silicon Valley, one imagines, probably already know this.
